extracted.intended_audience: aspiring essayists, translators, poets, and literate readers (early-18th-century periodical writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short periodical essays and literary translations in the manner of The Spectator: choice and use of mottos/quotations, rhetorical devices (signatures), qualities of poetic writing, and principles for faithful translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of motto / epigraph (prefer poets)
rubrics_metrics.description: When finishing a speculation, consider which ancient authors have touched upon the subject and choose a motto; the writer prefers taking mottos from the Poets rather than the Prose-writers, as the former generally give a finer turn to a Thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic mottos 'couch' thoughts in few words and harmonious numbers, making them portable to memory and adding 'Supernumerary Beauty' to a paper; a motto also helps when the Writer advances a Paradox by showing he is supported by good authorities. Caveat: mottos may be of little use to unlearned readers—treat them as 'a Word to the Wise' and ensure the body provides for readers who don't relish the motto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least one memorable line in each paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to furnish each paper with at least one good line from an ancient author (a 'motto' or striking quotation) so the reader meets 'at least one good Line in every Paper'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single striking line or image awakens the reader's imagination and gives the paper portable ornament; it also helps to prepossess readers in the writer's favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use learned quotations to increase perceived authority and popular appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations in Latin (or Greek) are effective: they make hearers/readers inquisitive and can draw larger audiences or increase a writer's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: country preachers quoting Latin drew greater congregations; small scraps of Latin at a paper's head can make common readers think the paper contains entertainment. The writer also notes that ladies are particularly pleased with Greek mottos. Use classical quotation strategically, but be mindful of obscurity for unlearned readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of signature letters / cabalistic marks as rhetorical ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing single capital letters (C, L, X, etc.) at the end of papers functions as an obscure mark to intrigue readers; the author uses such letters purposely as 'Charms' and amulets to preserve a paper from fascination and malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These marks serve as playful rhetorical devices to create mystery about authorship and character; the writer may vary letters (Q, Z, Y, 'Abracadabra') and need not fully explain them—obscurity itself can be an ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness in translation: preserve images, sentiments, ease and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation (illustrated by the translation of Sappho's ode) should preserve every image and sentiment of the original while having the ease and spirit of an original in the target language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator should retain the natural pathetick simplicity and harmonious turns where possible; acknowledge that translating ancients who lack 'unnatural Witticisms' is especially difficult, and success consists in conveying both content and the original's tone/energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical or ostentatious methods of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of artifices and modes of false wit: authors who boast of composing rapidly, who use mechanical tables or devices to 'make verses', or who treat wit as a thing to be manufactured are objects of satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an author who records the exact hours/days his pieces took; a 'poet' using tables ('poetical logarithms') to erect Latin verses; proposals for a 'Mill to make Verses'. The guidance is to prize genuine invention and authenticity over speed, contrivance, or public displays of mechanical cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good poetic writing follows nature and avoids petty conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: The best ancient lyric (e.g., Sappho) 'followed Nature in all her Thoughts, without descending to those little Points, Conceits, and Turns of Wit' that infect many modern lyrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor 'pathetick Simplicity' and genuine feeling over artificial turns of wit; avoid the affected ornaments that diminish natural sentiment and imagination in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical authorities to support paradoxes or uncommon opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: When advancing what may appear a Paradox to common minds, produce a motto or citation showing support from 'good Authorities' so the writer is not judged singular in his opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and allusions to respected ancient authors lend weight and protect the writer from charges of singularity; they also make paradoxes more palatable to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of literary ostentation undermining merit (speed and display)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ostentation about dispatch (boasting of rapid composition) or extravagant public displays (e.g., composing on glass with a diamond) are forms of false wit that prioritize show over genuine merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek praise for the speed or manner of producing work; true praise should rest on quality, not on the tricks or curious methods by which verses were contrived.
